editorial_policy: Curated factual summaries verified against linked WHO and CPCB pages, not a live scraped corpus; review when sources change.

sources.title: WHO global air quality guidelines
sources.fact: The WHO 2021 air quality guideline for PM2.5 is 5 micrograms per cubic metre as an annual average and 15 micrograms per cubic metre as a 24-hour average. These reference concentrations must be compared with measurements over the same averaging periods, not with a single instantaneous sensor reading.

sources.title: WHO global air quality guidelines
sources.fact: WHO 2021 recommends a PM10 annual average of 15 micrograms per cubic metre and a 24-hour average of 45 micrograms per cubic metre. A momentary PM10 value is not a valid direct test of either averaging-time guideline.

sources.title: WHO global air quality guidelines
sources.fact: WHO 2021 recommends an annual mean nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentration of 10 micrograms per cubic metre and a 24-hour mean of 25 micrograms per cubic metre. These are health-based concentration guidelines, not AQI values.

sources.title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines Q&A
sources.fact: Fine particles such as PM2.5 can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. WHO links air pollution with respiratory and cardiovascular harm. These population-level findings do not diagnose any individual or predict an individual's risk from a single reading.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: WHO identifies children, pregnant people, older adults, outdoor workers and people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions among groups at increased vulnerability or exposure. Individual advice should consider clinical circumstances and local official alerts.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: WHO recommends weighing the health benefits of activity against pollution exposure. During high-pollution episodes, sensitive people may need to reduce moderate or vigorous outdoor exertion and adapt activity timing or location. A lower forecast is not a guarantee of a safe outdoor window.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: Staying inside can lower outdoor pollution exposure, but actual indoor air depends on cooking, smoking, incense burning, building ventilation and pollution entering from outside. Outdoor AQI alone does not measure indoor concentrations, and ventilation decisions must consider safety.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: WHO reports that portable air cleaners can reduce indoor particles in studied settings, but health-outcome evidence and real-world effectiveness vary. Filter maintenance, cost, building ventilation and the device's suitability matter. Do not promise a fixed health benefit or percentage improvement for a household.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: Properly selected, certified and correctly fitted particle-filtering respirators can reduce inhalation of particles. Fit, correct use and individual suitability matter; no respirator guarantees protection, and people with respiratory conditions may need clinical advice.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: WHO emphasizes population-level reduction of pollution at its sources as the preferred strategy. Personal choices can help, but an individual's logged activity alone does not prove a specific amount of CO2 reduction, improved outdoor AQI or avoided disease.

sources.title: National Air Quality Index
sources.fact: India's CPCB National AQI categories are Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400), and Severe (401–500). These are CPCB AQI bands, not US AQI categories; the two index scales cannot be directly compared.

sources.title: National Air Quality Index
sources.fact: The CPCB describes increasing potential breathing discomfort as India's National AQI rises; its Severe category may affect healthy people and seriously affect people with existing diseases. Official local advisories and conditions should guide decisions.

sources.title: Air pollution: Personal interventions and risk communication
sources.fact: WHO notes there is no internationally harmonized AQI methodology. National indices use different thresholds and calculations, so they should not be directly compared or converted as though equivalent. Report pollutant concentrations and their measurement units and averaging times when available.
